bnf.note: BNF/BNFC is only available in the UK; not accessed.

items.t: Reducing urate/uric acid formation where deposition has occurred (gouty arthritis, tophi, nephrolithiasis) or is a predictable risk (e.g. malignancy treatment with risk of acute uric acid nephropathy); certain enzyme disorders; 2,8-DHA stones; recurrent mixed calcium oxalate stones with hyperuricosuria.

src.q: indicated for reducing urate/uric acid formation in conditions where urate/uric acid deposition has already occurred (e.g. gouty arthritis, skin tophi, nephrolithiasis) or is a predictable clinical risk
indicated for the management of recurrent mixed calcium oxalate renal stones in the presence of hyperuricosuria

items.t: Asymptomatic hyperuricaemia alone is generally not an indication.

src.q: Asymptomatic hyperuricaemia per se is generally not considered an indication for use of Zyloric.

items.t: NICE NG219: offer allopurinol or febuxostat first line for treat-to-target urate-lowering therapy; offer allopurinol first line in people with major cardiovascular disease (e.g. previous MI or stroke, unstable angina).

src.q: Offer either allopurinol or febuxostat as first-line treatment when starting treat-to-target ULT, taking into account the person's comorbidities and preferences.
Offer allopurinol as first-line treatment to people with gout who have major cardiovascular disease (for example, previous myocardial infarction or stroke, or unstable angina).

items.t: Adults: start low (e.g. 100 mg/day) and increase only if serum urate response is unsatisfactory. Suggested: 100-200 mg daily (mild), 300-600 mg daily (moderately severe), 700-900 mg daily (severe); or 2-10 mg/kg/day.

src.q: Allopurinol should be introduced at low dosage e.g. 100 mg/day to reduce the risk of adverse reactions and increased only if the serum urate response is unsatisfactory.
100 to 200 mg daily in mild conditions, 300 to 600 mg daily in moderately severe conditions, 700 to 900 mg daily in severe conditions.

items.t: NICE gout treat-to-target: start ULT at least 2-4 weeks after a flare settles (or during a flare if flares are frequent); start low and use monthly serum urate to guide increases; target below 360 micromol/litre (consider below 300 micromol/litre with tophi or ongoing flares).

src.q: Start ULT at least 2 to 4 weeks after a gout flare has settled. If flares are more frequent, ULT can be started during a flare
Start with a low dose of ULT and use monthly serum urate levels to guide dose increases, as tolerated, until the target serum urate level is reached.
Aim for a target serum urate level below 360 micromol/litre (6 mg/dl).

items.t: Flare prophylaxis when starting: SmPC advises an anti-inflammatory or colchicine for at least one month. NICE offers colchicine while reaching target (low-dose NSAID or corticosteroid if colchicine unsuitable).

src.q: it is advisable to give prophylaxis with a suitable anti-inflammatory agent or colchicine for at least one month
offer colchicine while the target serum urate level is being reached

items.t: Elderly: lowest dose that gives satisfactory urate reduction.

src.q: In the absence of specific data, the lowest dosage which produces satisfactory urate reduction should be used.

items.t: High urate turnover (e.g. before cytotoxic therapy): correct hyperuricaemia first, keep well hydrated, use the lower end of the dose range.

src.q: It is advisable to correct existing hyperuricaemia and/or hyperuricosuria with Zyloric before starting cytotoxic therapy.
Dosage of Zyloric should be at the lower end of the recommended dosage schedule.

items.t: Children under 15 years: 10-20 mg/kg/day, maximum 400 mg daily. Rarely indicated except in malignancy (especially leukaemia) and enzyme disorders such as Lesch-Nyhan syndrome.

src.q: Children under 15 years: 10 to 20 mg/kg bodyweight/day up to a maximum of 400 mg daily.
Use in children is rarely indicated, except in malignant conditions (especially leukaemia) and certain enzyme disorders such as Lesch-Nyhan syndrome.

items.t: Hypersensitivity to allopurinol or any excipient.

src.q: Zyloric should not be administered to individuals known to be hypersensitive to allopurinol or to any of the components of the formulation

items.t: Hypersensitivity (rash, DRESS, SJS/TEN) can occur at any time: stop immediately and do not rechallenge after hypersensitivity syndrome or SJS/TEN. Highest risk in the first weeks.

src.q: If such reactions occur at any time during treatment, allopurinol should be withdrawn immediately. Rechallenge should not be undertaken in patients with hypersensitivity syndrome and SJS/TEN.
The highest risk for SJS and TEN, or other serious hypersensitivity reactions, is within the first weeks of treatment.

items.t: HLA-B*5801: linked to hypersensitivity syndrome and SJS/TEN (up to 20% of Han Chinese, 8-15% Thai, about 12% Korean). Consider screening in high-prevalence groups; CKD adds risk. Known carriers: do not start unless no reasonable alternative and benefit outweighs risk. Negative result does not exclude SJS/TEN.

src.q: Screening for HLA-B*5801 should be considered before starting treatment with allopurinol in patient subgroups where the prevalence of this allele is known to be high.
allopurinol should not be started unless there are no other reasonable therapeutic options and the benefits are thought to exceed risks
SJS/TEN can still occur in patients who are found to be negative for HLA-B*5801 irrespective of their ethnic origin.

items.t: Chronic renal impairment with diuretics (especially thiazides): higher risk of hypersensitivity including SJS/TEN; extra vigilance.

src.q: Patients with chronic renal impairment and concomitant diuretic use, in particular thiazides, may be at increased risk of developing hypersensitivity reactions including SJS/TEN associated with allopurinol.

items.t: Use reduced doses in hepatic or renal impairment. Care in patients treated for hypertension or heart failure (e.g. diuretics, ACE inhibitors), who may have reduced renal function.

src.q: Reduced doses should be used in patients with hepatic or renal impairment
may have some concomitant impairment of renal function and allopurinol should be used with care in this group

items.t: Do not start until an acute gout attack has completely settled; flares can occur early in treatment. If a flare occurs on treatment, continue the same dose and treat the flare.

src.q: Allopurinol treatment should not be started until an acute attack of gout has completely subsided, as further attacks may be precipitated.
If acute attacks develop in patients receiving allopurinol, treatment should continue at the same dosage

items.t: Azathioprine or mercaptopurine: avoid the combination (fatal cases).

src.q: Concomitant use of allopurinol with 6-mercaptopurine or azathioprine should be avoided as there have been reports of fatal cases

items.t: Thyroid: raised TSH in long-term use; caution with altered thyroid function. Xanthine deposition possible with very high urate turnover (keep well hydrated). Contains lactose.

src.q: Caution is required when allopurinol is used in patients with alteration of thyroid function.
This risk may be minimised by adequate hydration to achieve optimal urine dilution.
Zyloric tablets contain lactose and therefore should not be administered to patients with rare hereditary problems of galactose intolerance

items.t: Azathioprine and mercaptopurine (not in this list): levels may reach toxic levels causing life-threatening pancytopenia. Avoid; if essential, give one quarter (25%) of the usual azathioprine/mercaptopurine dose with frequent blood counts.

src.q: Therefore, concomitant use of allopurinol with 6-mercaptopurine or azathioprine should be avoided.
dosing should be reduced to one quarter (25%) of the usual dose of 6-mercaptopurine or azathioprine and frequent haematologic monitoring should be ensured

items.t: Warfarin and other coumarins: rare reports of increased effect; monitor carefully.

src.q: There have been rare reports of increased effect of warfarin and other coumarin anticoagulants when co-administered with allopurinol, therefore, all patients receiving anticoagulants must be carefully monitored.

items.t: Ampicillin or amoxicillin: more skin rash; use an alternative where available.

src.q: it is recommended that in patients receiving allopurinol an alternative to ampicillin or amoxicillin is used where available

items.t: Diuretics (especially thiazides) and ACE inhibitors: increased risk of hypersensitivity, especially in renal impairment. Furosemide may raise serum urate and oxipurinol.

src.q: An increased risk of hypersensitivity has been reported when allopurinol is given with diuretics, in particular thiazides, especially in renal impairment.
An increased risk of hypersensitivity has been reported when allopurinol is given with ACE inhibitors especially in renal impairment.

items.t: Aluminium hydroxide: may reduce allopurinol effect; separate by at least 3 hours.

src.q: If aluminium hydroxide is taken concomitantly, allopurinol may have an attenuated effect. There should be an interval of at least 3 hours between taking both medicines.

items.t: Others: large-dose salicylates and uricosurics may reduce effect; chlorpropamide in renal impairment (prolonged hypoglycaemia); theophylline (monitor levels); ciclosporin (toxicity); didanosine (not recommended); cytostatics (blood dyscrasias, monitor counts); vidarabine; phenytoin.

src.q: drugs with uricosuric activity such as probenecid or large doses of salicylate may accelerate the excretion of oxipurinol
Theophylline levels should be monitored in patients starting or increasing allopurinol therapy.
Co-administration of these 2 drugs is generally not recommended.

items.t: Allopurinol and metabolites accumulate in renal impairment; reduced doses required. Severe renal insufficiency: consider less than 100 mg per day or 100 mg at intervals longer than one day. The SmPC gives no CrCl/eGFR cut-offs. If available, keep plasma oxipurinol below 100 micromol/litre.

src.q: In severe renal insufficiency, it may be advisable to use less than 100 mg per day or to use single doses of 100 mg at longer intervals than one day.
the dose should be adjusted to maintain plasma oxipurinol levels below 100 micromol/litre (15.2 mg/litre)
A reduction in the dose of Zyloric is therefore required in patients with renal impairment.

items.t: Dialysis two to three times a week: consider 300-400 mg immediately after each dialysis, none in between.

src.q: If dialysis is required two to three times a week consideration should be given to an alternative dosage schedule of 300-400 mg Zyloric immediately after each dialysis with none in the interim.

items.t: NICE: offer urate-lowering therapy (treat-to-target) in CKD stages 3 to 5; consider rheumatology referral for CKD stages 3b to 5.

src.q: CKD stages 3 to 5 (glomerular filtration rate [GFR] categories G3 to G5)
they have CKD stages 3b to 5 (GFR categories G3b to G5)

items.t: Use reduced doses in hepatic impairment; periodic liver function tests in early treatment.

src.q: Reduced doses should be used in patients with hepatic impairment. Periodic liver function tests are recommended during the early stages of therapy.

items.t: SmPC: inadequate evidence of safety; use only when there is no safer alternative and the disease itself carries risk.

src.q: Use in pregnancy only when there is no safer alternative and when the disease itself carries risks for the mother or unborn child.

items.t: BUMPS: can be used in pregnancy if recommended by a specialist; limited data, two babies with similar unusual birth defects reported.

src.q: Allopurinol can be used in pregnancy if recommended by a specialist.
two babies exposed in the womb to allopurinol were born with similar unusual birth defects

items.t: Allopurinol and oxipurinol pass into breast milk; effects on the baby unknown. Not recommended during breastfeeding (SmPC). No SPS breastfeeding page found.

src.q: Allopurinol and its metabolite oxipurinol is excreted in the human breast milk.
Allopurinol during breastfeeding is not recommended.

items.t: Male infertility and erectile dysfunction reported very rarely. BUMPS: no evidence that use by the father harms the baby.

src.q: Reproductive system and breast disorders Very rare Infertility male Erectile dysfunction
There is no evidence that allopurinol used by the father can harm the baby through effects on the sperm.

items.t: Common: rash; raised TSH. Uncommon: nausea, vomiting, diarrhoea, abnormal liver tests, hypersensitivity.

src.q: Skin and subcutaneous tissue disorders Common Rash
Investigations Common Blood thyroid stimulating hormone increased

items.t: Severe skin and hypersensitivity reactions (SJS/TEN, DRESS with fever, rash, eosinophilia, liver or kidney involvement): stop immediately and permanently; do not re-introduce.

src.q: If such reactions occur at any time during treatment, allopurinol should be withdrawn immediately and permanently.
If SJS/TEN, or other serious hypersensitivity reactions cannot be ruled out, DO NOT re-introduce allopurinol due to the potential for a severe or even fatal reaction.

items.t: After a mild rash only, may re-introduce at a small dose (e.g. 50 mg/day); stop permanently if rash recurs.

src.q: After recovery from mild reactions, Zyloric may, if desired, be re-introduced at a small dose (e.g. 50 mg/day) and gradually increased.

items.t: Very rare: agranulocytosis, aplastic anaemia, thrombocytopenia (especially with renal or hepatic impairment); hepatitis (rare).

src.q: Very rare reports have been received of thrombocytopenia, agranulocytosis and aplastic anaemia, particularly in individuals with impaired renal and/or hepatic function

items.t: Consider HLA-B*5801 screening before starting in high-prevalence groups (Han Chinese, Thai, Korean).

src.q: Screening for HLA-B*5801 should be considered before starting treatment with allopurinol in patient subgroups where the prevalence of this allele is known to be high.

items.t: Adjust dose by serum urate and urinary urate at intervals (NICE: monthly during titration; consider annual check once at target). Periodic LFTs early in treatment if hepatic impairment.

src.q: The dosage should be adjusted by monitoring serum urate concentrations and urinary urate/uric acid levels at appropriate intervals.
Consider annual monitoring of serum urate level in people with gout who are continuing ULT after reaching their target serum urate level.

items.t: Stop immediately at any sign of hypersensitivity or severe skin reaction.

src.q: Zyloric should be withdrawn immediately should such reactions occur.

items.t: Once daily after a meal. If the dose is above 300 mg/day and there is GI upset, divide the dose.

src.q: Zyloric may be taken orally once a day after a meal.
Should the daily dosage exceed 300 mg and gastrointestinal intolerance be manifested, a divided doses regimen may be appropriate.

items.t: Stop and seek help at once if a rash, fever, blistering, mouth sores or swollen glands appear.

src.q: the patient should be informed of the need to stop treatment immediately at the first appearance of symptoms

items.t: Usually lifelong once target urate is reached (NICE). Keep taking it during a gout flare.

src.q: Ensure people understand that ULT is usually continued after the target serum urate level is reached, and is typically a lifelong treatment.

items.t: May cause drowsiness, vertigo or unsteadiness: take care driving until you know how it affects you.

src.q: Since adverse reactions such as somnolence, vertigo and ataxia have been reported in patients receiving allopurinol
